newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin urges Security Council to back new vision.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin urges Security Council to back new vision.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin opened a meeting of his policy-making Security Council on Wednesday that is expected to approve a document laying out a new vision of Russia's security needs into the 21st century.
"This is a matter of crucial significance and very important not only for the state but for all Russian society, for all the Russian people," Russian news agencies quoted Yeltsin as saying.

"I think we will approve it," he said of the document, which lays down a whole new conception of the country's priorities and will play a part in Yeltsin's efforts to trim and modernise Russia's vast but impoverished Soviet-era armed forces.

Itar-Tass news agency quoted a Security Council official saying the four-part document, worked out over the past year, concluded that the main threats Russia faced for the foreseeable future were not so much military as social and economic.

As a result, the document said priorities for improving national security were "strengthening social stability" and completing and developing notions of statehood and federalism as well as returning to economic growth.

Interfax news agency quoted Yeltsin as telling the Council, which includes the prime minister and his first deputies and several ministers including those of defence, interior and justice, that the government's responsibilities had increased with the planned expansion of NATO into eastern Europe.
"What should we be in future? Either leave ourselves open or give ourselves better cover in the East? We have to think seriously about this," the agency quoted Yeltsin as saying.

It was not clear whether the president was referring to improving Russia's defences in eastern Europe -- to Moscow's west -- or forging better ties with its eastern neighbours, like China. Both are strategies the Kremlin has considered.
Yeltsin told Krasnaya Zvezda, the armed forces newspaper, in an interview on Wednesday that he would do everything possible to minimise the consequences of NATO expansion.

He pledged to improve the economic lot of service personnel while promoting a transition to a smaller, better-trained professional army without conscription. He also criticised the slow pace of reform in the armed forces.
The Defence Ministry has complained that government defence cuts forced this month by a 40 percent shortfall in tax revenues risked undermining the nation's security.
The armed forces are preparing for festivities on Friday, May 9, celebrating the 52nd anniversary of the 1945 victory over Nazi Germany.
